Speak to your optician if the coating on your lenses appears to be crazing - a fine network of cracks rather than isolated scratches - or if it is hazing, lifting or separating at the edges. Those are coating failures rather than wear, and depending on the lens's age and how it was supplied they may be worth raising with the supplier instead of simply replacing. If you work around abrasive dust, metal particles or solvents, say so when you order: the right answer may be a different lens material or purpose-made safety eyewear rather than a better coating on a standard lens. And if your vision is reduced by a haze you cannot clean off, have the lenses examined before concluding that the coating is the whole story.

title: How Photochromic Lenses Work: Why They Darken in UV and Stay Clear in a Car
meta_description: Photochromic lenses darken because ultraviolet triggers a reversible chemical change, not because it is bright. Why a car windscreen defeats them and heat limits them.
body_html:
Why a photochromic lens is not a brightness sensor

Most people assume photochromic lenses darken because it is bright outside. They do not. They darken because ultraviolet radiation reaches them. The trigger is a specific band of the spectrum, not the visible brightness you perceive, and that single fact explains almost everything people find strange about these lenses.

The mechanism is a reversible chemical change inside the lens. In the organic photochromic lenses that dominate the market, the active ingredients are dye molecules - naphthopyrans and related compounds - dispersed through the lens material. At rest these molecules are transparent to visible light. When ultraviolet photons arrive they supply enough energy to rearrange bonds within the molecule, producing a form that absorbs visible light strongly and therefore looks grey or brown. When the ultraviolet goes away the molecule relaxes back to its original shape and the lens clears.

Two terms matter. Photochromism is the name for a light-induced, reversible colour change. Activation is the darkening step and fading (or bleaching) is the return to clear. Both are chemistry, not electronics, and neither is under your control.

Two technologies, one behaviour

Photochromic lenses come in two chemistries. In mineral glass, tiny silver halide crystals are distributed through the material; ultraviolet drives a reversible silver reaction that darkens the glass - a mechanism related to the chemistry of old photographic film. In plastic lenses, now the norm, the same effect has to be produced with organic dye molecules, because the silver chemistry depends on the glass matrix.

The practical consequences differ. Glass photochromic lenses tend to fade more slowly and to hold their darkness better as temperature rises, because the inorganic reaction is less heat-sensitive. Plastic lenses are lighter, safer and available in higher indices, but rely on the organic chemistry with its temperature dependence. Neither is strictly better; they are differently balanced.

Why they go clear inside a car

This is the most common complaint and it has a precise cause: car glass is formulated to block ultraviolet. Windscreen glass in particular is specified to filter the large majority of UV, with figures around 99% commonly quoted for the laminated glass used in windscreens. No ultraviolet, no activation.

So a photochromic lens worn while driving stays close to clear even in strong sun, and this is not a fault - it is the design working as specified. If you need a genuinely dark lens while driving, you have two options: a lens whose photochromic system also responds to visible light (newer generations do, and cost considerably more), or a fixed tint. It is worth reading our comparison of photochromic lenses and prescription sunglasses before deciding which of the two you actually want, because they solve different problems.

Why they never get as dark as the shop suggested

Temperature. The fade reaction competes with the activation reaction, and heat pushes the balance back towards the clear state. A photochromic lens therefore darkens less on a hot day than a cold one, under identical ultraviolet. In summer heat you may get a mid-grey rather than the dark tint the sample showed you under a UV lamp in an air-conditioned shop.

This is also why the same lens can look impressively dark on a cold ski slope and disappointing at the beach. Nothing has changed except the temperature.

Activation and fade are not instantaneous

Both steps take time, and the asymmetry between them is what most annoys wearers. Activation is relatively quick: the lens begins to darken within seconds of ultraviolet exposure and usually reaches most of its density in well under a minute. Fading is slower, because it is a thermal relaxation process - the molecule has to find its way back to the resting shape, and that happens faster when it is warm and slower when it is cold. On a cold day, walking from bright sun into a dim interior, you can be left wearing a lens that stays visibly tinted for several minutes.

Common misconceptions

  • "They darken in any bright light." They respond primarily to ultraviolet. A very bright but UV-poor source - much indoor lighting, a screen, or sunlight through a car windscreen - will barely activate them.
  • "Darker means more UV protection." The dangerous one. UV protection and tint depth are separate properties. A photochromic lens should be blocking UV even in its clear state; the darkness is a comfort feature, not the protection. Read the UV claim, not the tint.
  • "They last forever." Organic photochromic dyes degrade with cumulative UV exposure. Over years both the maximum darkness and the fading speed decline, and the lens may hold a faint residual tint when it should be clear. That is ageing, not a defect.
  • "They replace sunglasses." Behind glass they are not dark at all, and they cannot match a fixed dark tint across a full day of bright sun. They suit people who move constantly between indoors and outdoors.

When to ask a professional

Raise it with a dispensing optician before ordering if you drive long distances in daylight, work outdoors in high heat, or need a reliably dark lens for a specific activity - in each case the chemistry works against you and a fixed tint is usually the better answer. Mention it too if you have a condition that makes you light-sensitive: the depth of darkening a photochromic lens delivers is neither adjustable nor guaranteed, and a medical need is better met with something predictable. If a photochromic lens stops darkening well before you would expect, say so - the dye may simply have reached the end of its useful life.

title: How Polarized Lenses Cut Glare: The Physics of Reflected Light
meta_description: Glare off water and roads is strongly polarised, and a polarising filter blocks it. What the Brewster angle tells us, and what polarised lenses cannot do.
body_html:
Glare is not just brightness - it has an orientation

Walk along water on a bright day and the surface throws a harsh, almost metallic sheet of light at you. That light is not simply strong. It is polarised, and polarisation is a property of how the light wave oscillates.

Light is a transverse wave: its electric field oscillates perpendicular to the direction it travels. In ordinary sunlight those oscillations point in every direction at random, and the light is said to be unpolarised. But when light reflects off a flat, non-metallic surface - water, snow, wet asphalt, a car bonnet - the reflection process preferentially favours one orientation. The reflected light ends up with its electric field oscillating largely parallel to the reflecting surface, which for a horizontal surface means horizontally polarised. That is glare.

Why a polarising filter works, and at which angle

A polarising filter is a sheet of stretched polymer loaded with aligned molecules. It transmits light oscillating along one axis and absorbs light oscillating perpendicular to it. Sunglass polarisers are oriented so that axis is vertical - the same orientation as most of the light coming from the scene in front of you, and perpendicular to the horizontally polarised glare coming off a horizontal surface. The glare is blocked; the scene is not.

Reflection polarises light most completely at a particular incidence angle, the Brewster angle, where the reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular to each other. For water, whose refractive index is about 1.33 in the visible range, the Brewster angle is approximately 53 degrees from the surface normal. In practice the effect is useful over a wide band rather than a single angle: measurements of sunlight glinting off water find the glint is at least 90% polarised for incidence angles between roughly 45 and 61 degrees. That is why a polarising filter is so effective looking across water at a shallow angle - a fisherman's view, or a driver's view along a wet road.

What that means in practice

  • Wet roads and water. Glare from horizontal surfaces is precisely the orientation a polariser is built to reject, so this is where the benefit is largest and most obvious.
  • Snow and pale sand. These reflect a very large fraction of incoming light, and that light is partly polarised, so a polariser cuts the wash that flattens detail.
  • Depth perception. Because polarised glare masks the structure of what lies behind it, removing it often restores texture - lane markings, ripples, the surface of a bench.
  • The sky is not uniform. Skylight becomes polarised at roughly 90 degrees from the sun. A polariser can darken that band noticeably, which photographers use deliberately and which some wearers find uneven.

What a polarising filter physically is

A polarised sunglass lens is not a tinted lens with an extra coating. The filter is a separate film, conventionally a stretched polymer sheet - typically polyvinyl alcohol treated with iodine - that is then drawn so its long molecular chains line up in one direction. Aligned molecules absorb light oscillating along one axis and transmit the perpendicular axis. The film is bonded into the lens as an internal layer, which is why polarised lenses are built as a laminate rather than simply dyed.

That construction has consequences. The film adds an internal interface, so a polarised lens is generally a little thicker than an equivalent non-polarised one. It also means the polariser sits inside the lens rather than on its surface: a surface scuff may polish out, but damage that reaches the film itself is not something to expect to repair. On the plus side, modern lamination is far more resistant to edge delamination than the early polarising films were.

Common misconceptions

  • "Polarised means more UV protection." Polarisation and UV filtering are separate functions performed by different parts of the lens. A polarised lens is not automatically a UV-filtering lens, and a UV400 lens need not be polarised at all. The two are often sold together, which is where the confusion starts.
  • "Polarised lenses reduce the total light by half." They do not halve the light; a polariser absorbs the component oscillating along one axis. Because ordinary light is randomly oriented, roughly half of it is lost in principle - but polarisers are not ideal, and the visible effect depends strongly on what you are looking at. The benefit is not a uniform dimming, it is selective rejection of one orientation.
  • "Polarised is always better." It has real costs. Polarisation interacts with LCD displays, making some instrument panels, dashboard screens and phone displays hard to read or markedly darker when viewed at particular angles. If you rely on a screen outdoors, try before you buy.
  • "It fixes UV, glare and brightness all at once." Three different problems. Tint depth handles brightness; the UV treatment handles radiation; polarisation handles orientation. A pair can do all three, but one feature does not imply another.

When to ask a professional

Ask a dispensing optician if you need polarised lenses for a specific use - sailing, fishing, driving, skiing, or any sport with a bright reflective surface - so the tint category and the polariser can be chosen together rather than as an afterthought. Mention it as well if you notice that glare is still uncomfortable despite dark lenses, because tint alone will not address polarised glare no matter how dark it is. If you take your sunglasses on the water or into snow, light reaching the eye from the sides and around the frame matters as much as the lens itself, so coverage is worth discussing at the same time as the filter.

title: Office Progressive Lenses: Why Standard Progressives Fail at a Desk
meta_description: A standard progressive is built for distance and reading, not for a screen at arm's length. What degression changes, and the maths of working distance.
body_html:
A progressive lens is built around an assumption, and the assumption is where you look

A general-purpose progressive lens is a single surface carrying three optical zones stacked vertically. The upper part is the distance zone, ground for looking at things far away. The lower part is the near zone, ground to add plus power for close work. Between them runs a narrow transition band, usually called the corridor or intermediate zone, where the power changes progressively from one to the other.

That design is a set of compromises, and the compromise that matters most at a desk is the width of the corridor. A general-purpose progressive has to give away enough of the lens to distance and near that the middle band stays relatively narrow. It works well for the way most people use glasses: look up to see across a room, look down to read. It works badly for the way most people use a computer, which is to hold a fixed gaze at an intermediate distance for hours.

Where your screen actually sits, in dioptres

Working distance and lens power are linked by a simple relationship: power in dioptres equals one divided by the distance in metres. That single equation explains the whole problem.

  • A near addition of +2.00 D is ground to bring the near point to 1 / 2.00 = 0.50 m, that is 50 cm.
  • An addition of +2.50 D corresponds to 40 cm; +1.50 D to roughly 67 cm.
  • Reading a book is typically done somewhere around 35 to 45 cm. A desktop monitor usually sits further out, commonly in the region of 50 to 70 cm, with a laptop closer and a large screen further.

So if your addition is +2.50 D and your screen is at 65 cm, the screen is not where your lens is sharpest. To read it clearly you either push the screen closer, lean in, or tip your head up to find the corridor. All three are common, and all three are uncomfortable over a working day.

What an office or occupational lens changes

Occupational lenses - sold under various names such as office, desk, near-variable or indoor progressives - start from a different assumption: that the wearer is indoors, looking at things between roughly arm's length and a few metres. The design response is to reduce the power range between the top and bottom of the lens and to spend the space that frees up on a much wider intermediate zone.

The reduced top-to-bottom power change is usually described as degression: instead of running all the way from plano to the full near addition, the lens degresses only part of the way. That buys corridor width and comfortable distance vision out to a few metres, at the cost of clear distance vision beyond that. An office lens is not designed for driving or for watching television across a room, and that limitation is the whole point of the trade.

They are fitted differently, too

An occupational lens is not simply a different design sitting in the same position in the frame. Because its zones are laid out differently, it is fitted with a different vertical position and often a different corridor length, and the height at which your pupil sits relative to the lens matters more, not less. That makes the frame part of the optics rather than a separate decision: a shallow frame may not have the vertical depth to hold an intermediate-dominant design comfortably, while an unusually deep frame can leave your habitual gaze sitting above the zone the lens was built to put there. It is the practical reason office lenses are usually discussed together with the frame rather than ordered afterwards and squeezed into a pair you already own.

Common misconceptions

  • "Any progressive works fine at a desk." A general-purpose progressive will work, but you will be using its narrowest zone for your longest-held gaze. That is why so many people describe screen work as the least comfortable part of wearing their first pair.
  • "Computer glasses means blue-light glasses." These are unrelated. An occupational lens solves a geometry problem - where the correction is placed on the lens for a particular working distance. A blue-light coating addresses a spectral question. Asking for the first will not get you the second, and a blue-light coating does not widen the corridor.
  • "A stronger reading addition will make the screen sharper." Only if the screen is at the distance that addition is ground for. Increasing the addition when the screen is too far away makes the mismatch worse, not better - the dioptre-to-distance relationship runs both ways.
  • "Office lenses are an upgrade over normal progressives." They are a specialisation. If you need one pair for everything, an occupational lens will let you down at distance.

When to ask a professional

Ask a dispensing optician if you spend several hours a day at a screen and find yourself tilting your head, leaning in, or holding a monitor closer than is comfortable. The most useful thing you can bring is a measurement rather than an opinion: the actual distance from your eye to the screen, in centimetres, measured in your normal sitting position. That number, next to your prescription and your current addition, tells the optician whether a general-purpose progressive is simply ground for a working distance you never actually use. Also raise it if you already wear progressives and notice that the screen is the one thing that never feels properly in focus, because that is a fitting question rather than an adaptation problem, and no amount of perseverance will fix a corridor that points at the wrong distance.

title: Why Lenses Fog and How Anti-Fog Coatings Actually Work
meta_description: Fogging is condensation, not dirt, and coatings fight it by changing how water spreads. Why hydrophilic and hydrophobic surfaces behave so differently on a lens.
body_html:
Fog is condensation, and the droplets - not the water - are the problem

When you come in from the cold, or breathe out behind a face covering, the air next to your face is warm and carries a lot of water vapour. The lens surface is cooler. Air can only hold a certain amount of water vapour at a given temperature, and that limit falls as the temperature falls. When the lens drops below the dew point of the air around it, the excess vapour has to go somewhere, and it condenses onto the surface.

What you then see is not a layer of water in the ordinary sense. It is thousands of microscopic droplets, each one a tiny lens that scatters incoming light in every direction. That scattering is the white veil. The crucial insight for everything that follows is that water is not the problem. A continuous, uniform film of water is almost perfectly transparent. Discrete droplets are not.

Two ways to defeat fogging, and only one of them suits a spectacle lens

Surface behaviour with water is described by the contact angle - the angle a droplet makes with the surface where they meet. It is the standard measurable quantity in this field: a high contact angle means the droplet sits up and beads; a low one means the water spreads out flat. Every anti-fog strategy is really a decision about which way you want the water to behave.

  • Hydrophilic - water spreading. A water-attracting surface lowers the contact angle so that condensed water merges into a continuous sheet instead of standing in droplets. Because a sheet does not scatter light the way droplets do, the lens stays clear. This is the principle behind most anti-fog treatments and coatings for spectacle lenses, and it is the approach that directly answers the physics of the problem.
  • Hydrophobic to superhydrophobic - water shedding. A strongly water-repelling surface makes droplets bead and run off, which is excellent for rain on a windscreen or a jacket. For fog on a lens the mechanism is different and less direct: the aim is to make droplets coalesce and shed before they build into a veil. It is a real research area, but it is not the mechanism used by ordinary anti-fog spectacle coatings.

The distinction matters when you buy treatments, because a product that makes your lenses shed water beautifully is not necessarily one that stops them fogging, and the two are marketed with very similar words.

Why your anti-reflective lenses fog so readily

Anti-reflective coating stacks are normally finished with a hydrophobic and oleophobic top layer. That layer earns its place: it repels oil from fingerprints and water from rain, and it makes the lens easier to clean. But it is water-repellent by design, which means condensed water sits on it as droplets rather than spreading. Add the two other factors always present in spectacle wear - the lens is very close to a warm, moist source of air, and it is thin enough to cool quickly - and a treated lens can fog eagerly.

This is why anti-fog performance is often better on a plain lens than on a fully coated one, and why aftermarket anti-fog treatments work by overriding the hydrophobic top layer rather than cooperating with it.

How anti-fog performance is actually judged

Fogging resistance is not a matter of opinion in occupational eyewear. There is a defined test method, EN 168, which sets out how the fogging behaviour of personal eye protection is assessed, and EN 166, which states the performance requirements such products must meet. When a product is sold as fog-resistant for safety use, that is the framework it is being measured against. Consumer sunglasses and fashion eyewear are not generally held to it, which is one reason the same claim means very different things in different shops.

Common misconceptions

  • "Anti-fog coating lasts as long as the lens." Generally it does not. Built-in coatings are more durable than sprays and cloths, but liquid and wipe-on treatments must be reapplied, and every cleaning cycle removes some of the layer.
  • "Rubbing the lens clear solves it." It smears the water around and often makes the surface temporarily worse, because the moisture has not gone anywhere. The lens is usually clearest once the water has been allowed to spread or evaporate.
  • "If it fogs, it must be dirty." Not necessarily. Fogging is driven by temperature and humidity, and a spotless lens fogs perfectly well in a cold doorway.
  • "Anti-fog and anti-reflective are the same kind of coating." Different jobs: anti-reflective addresses reflection using thin-film interference, anti-fog addresses condensation using surface energy. One does not imply the other.
  • "Hot water is the safest way to clean and de-fog." Hot water is hard on coating stacks. Lukewarm water and a clean cloth are kinder to a lens you want to keep.

When to ask a professional

Raise it with an optician if fogging is constant, if it affects one eye far more than the other, or if it comes with pain, redness, discharge or a persistently gritty feeling. Fogging is usually a physics problem, but a tear film that is not working properly can make the surface of the eye itself behave badly, and that is for an eye care professional rather than a better cloth. If you wear a face covering or work in a setting where eye protection is required, mention it: the fitting of the covering and the specification of the eyewear both affect the outcome, and occupational eyewear is expected to be tested against the fogging standard rather than marketed with a slogan. And if you keep buying anti-fog treatments without success, describe exactly when the fogging happens - the fix tends to be specific to the situation, not universal.

title: The Three Numbers Inside Your Glasses Arm, Explained
meta_description: Those small numbers on the temple arm are the frame's own dimensions. What A, B, DBL, ED and temple length mean, and how they change your lenses.
body_html:
Why a frame carries measurements at all

A spectacle frame is not one size. It is a set of dimensions, and those dimensions decide not only how the frame fits but what the lenses inside it have to be. The numbers stamped inside the temple arm exist so that anyone - you, or a different optician three years later - can order an equivalent frame without measuring it by hand.

The system behind them is called the boxing system, and it is worth knowing because it is the vocabulary every optician uses. A rectangle is imagined around the lens shape, with its sides touching the widest and tallest points of the rim. Everything is then measured from that box.

  • A (eye size) - the horizontal width of the box in millimetres. This is the first number on the arm.
  • B - the vertical height of the box. Usually not stamped, but it matters: it controls how much depth of lens you have for a progressive corridor.
  • DBL (distance between lenses) - the gap between the two boxes, which is what most people call the bridge width. The second number.
  • ED (effective diameter) - the diameter of the smallest circle that fully contains the lens shape. Not the same as A in any frame that is not a perfect circle.
  • Temple length - the third number, measured from the frame front to the tip of the side arm.

The number that actually changes your lenses

Add A to DBL and you get the frame PD - the horizontal distance between the geometric centres of the two lens shapes. It is the frame's own pupil distance, and it is rarely the same as yours. That difference is the decentration, and it is where frame choice quietly becomes an optical decision.

Decentration per eye = (frame PD - your PD) / 2

Two consequences follow. First, thickness: the further the lens has to be shifted to centre it on your pupil, the further off-centre your pupil sits within the blank, and the more edge thickness you end up with at a given power. Second, and less obvious, the minimum blank size the lab must start from:

Minimum blank size = ED + (2 x decentration) + 2 mm

That 2 mm is edging allowance. If the required blank is larger than the blanks made in your chosen material and index, the job cannot be produced in that material at all - which is why a large, angular frame combined with a narrow pupil distance sometimes forces a change of index or a different frame entirely.

Why this is not just a cosmetic detail

A frame that is too wide for your pupils does not merely look off-centre; it changes the optics. Unwanted prism increases with both decentration and the power of the lens, which is one reason a strong prescription can feel uncomfortable in a large frame that behaves perfectly well with a mild one. And because decentration interacts with index and thickness, the thin-lens upgrade that solved a thickness problem in one frame may be unnecessary in a narrower one.

It is also why moving lenses into a new frame is not the same as re-ordering the same frame. If A and DBL change, the decentration changes, and with it the fit of the lens to your pupil. You can estimate the thickness consequence of that change before committing to an index upgrade using our free lens thickness calculator.

Temple length is about fit, not optics

Temple length is the one number among the three with no optical role. It controls where the arm ends behind your ear and therefore whether the frame sits at the right height and angle on your face. A frame that is optically well matched but two millimetres short on the temple will slide forward - and a frame that slides changes its own optics, because the vertex distance and the effective power of the lens change as it moves away from the eye. When you compare a frame's numbers against one you already own, match the temple length first; A and DBL are the numbers that change the lenses.

Common misconceptions

  • "54-18-140 means the frame is 54 mm wide." No. 54 is the width of one lens box, not the frame. The total front width includes the bridge and the end pieces and is usually much larger.
  • "Any frame can take my prescription." Not automatically. Minimum blank size, decentration and the blanks available in a given material all constrain what can be made, most sharply at high powers.
  • "The numbers are universal." The boxing system is standard practice, but not every frame is marked, and cheaper frames sometimes omit a number. If one is missing, have the frame measured rather than guessed.
  • "A bigger frame gives more room for progressives." More B measurement does help a fitting height, but a wider frame increases decentration, which adds thickness and can add unwanted prism. Size is a trade-off in both directions.

When to ask a dispensing optician

Ask before you buy if your prescription is strong in either direction, if your pupil distance is notably narrow or wide for your face, if you are choosing a large or heavily curved frame, or if you wear a progressive and need a usable fitting height. Ask as well if the same prescription has felt different in different frames - that is usually decentration and vertex distance at work, not imagination. And bring the frame's numbers with you when comparing options online: A, DBL and temple length are the only reliable way to compare two frames across sellers, because a frame described only as medium tells you nothing you can check.

title: How Anti-Reflective Coatings Work: The Physics Behind the Purple-Green Sheen
meta_description: Anti-reflective coatings cancel reflected light by interference, not absorption. The optics behind the colour you see, and what the coating cannot do for you.
body_html:
Why an uncoated lens throws light back at you

Every time light crosses from one transparent medium into another, part of it bounces back. How much depends on the size of the jump in refractive index between the two materials: the bigger the mismatch, the stronger the reflection. A plastic lens with an index near 1.5 meets air at about 1.0, and that difference sends roughly 8 per cent of the light arriving at each surface straight back towards the wearer. Two surfaces, front and back, and you have two sources of unwanted reflection before you have even considered scratches.

You have seen the consequences. The faint image of your own eye floating over the page you are reading. Halos and streaks around headlights at night. A bright window reflected in the middle of a screen you are trying to see past. None of that is dirt, and none of it is a defect. It is the physics of an index mismatch, and it cannot be wiped away.

The cure is interference, not absorption

An anti-reflective coating does not soak up the reflected light. It cancels it. The trick is to place a thin transparent layer on the surface so that light reflected from the top of that layer and light reflected from its underside emerge out of step with one another and extinguish each other.

The governing idea is the quarter-wave condition. If a layer's optical thickness - its physical thickness multiplied by its refractive index - equals one quarter of the wavelength of the light, then the two reflections come back half a wavelength out of phase and cancel. Note that the condition is stated in optical thickness, not physical thickness. A layer a quarter-wave thick for green light is not a quarter-wave layer for red, which is the whole reason the colour you see in the coating matters.

Two refinements turn this from a curiosity into a workable product. First, the layer's own refractive index should sit between that of air and that of the lens, roughly in the middle, so that its two reflected waves are of comparable strength. Waves of very different strength cancel only partly, however perfectly they are aligned in phase. Second, a single quarter-wave layer can only be tuned to cancel well near one wavelength. Practical coatings are therefore multilayer stacks: several layers of different indices and thicknesses, each tuned to a different part of the visible spectrum, so that residual reflection stays low across the whole range instead of only in the middle of it. Requirements and test methods for these coatings are specified in the ISO 8980 series; ISO 8980-4 deals specifically with anti-reflective coatings for uncut finished spectacle lenses.

Why the coating looks purple, green or blue

That colour is the residue, not the design. Because cancellation is never perfect at every wavelength at once, the light that survives is whatever was not cancelled - typically a narrow band in the violet-green-blue region. That is exactly why an AR-coated lens shows a faint purple or green sheen when you tilt it under a light. The sheen is a signature of the interference stack, and a good coating is judged by how faint and neutral that residue is, not by its absence.

Why the layers are stacked in a particular order

The order is not arbitrary, because each layer has to bond to the one beneath it and survive the ones above. The hard coat goes directly onto the lens substrate, since its job is to give a soft polymer surface a durable base. The anti-reflective stack is built on top of the hard coat. The hydrophobic and oleophobic layer goes last, because it must present the outward-facing surface - and would prevent anything else bonding to it if it were buried underneath. Layer thicknesses are controlled to fractions of a wavelength of visible light, which makes coating the most tolerance-sensitive step in making a lens, and means a coating line is judged on consistency rather than on its best sample.

What an anti-reflective coating cannot do

It does not make a lens scratch-resistant, it does not protect against impact, and it does not filter ultraviolet radiation. Those are separate functions: the hard coat beneath it, the lens material itself, and a specific UV-absorbing treatment. An AR coating is also not the same thing as a blue-light filter. Anti-reflective coatings work by cancelling reflections across the spectrum; a blue-light filter deliberately transmits less light in a chosen part of the spectrum. They solve different problems, even though both are described to shoppers using the word filter.

Common misconceptions

  • "The green sheen means the coating is cheap." Not a reliable test. Some visible sheen is expected on any interference coating. What matters is whether reflection is genuinely reduced when you look through the lens.
  • "AR coating blocks glare from headlights." It reduces reflections and the halos they cause, which does help at night, but it does not dim a bright light source.
  • "AR coating is what makes lenses easy to clean." Conventional stacks usually end with a hydrophobic and oleophobic layer for exactly that reason, but they are distinct layers and each can exist without the other.
  • "The coating is permanent." Coatings wear with time and cleaning. A coating that is hazing, crazing or lifting at the edges is a coating failure worth raising, rather than evidence that you cleaned it wrongly.

When to ask a professional

Ask if night driving glare remains a persistent problem despite coated lenses, because the cause may be an uncorrected prescription or another optical factor rather than coating quality. Ask too if coatings on previous pairs failed early - the right answer is often a different lens material or coating specification rather than simply replacing the lenses again. And if reflections are worst when you are reading at a screen, mention your working distance and screen position as well, since cutting reflected light and reducing the effort your eyes are making are two different interventions.

title: How to Read the Markings on Safety Eyewear: EN 166, EN 170 and EN 172
meta_description: The letters and numbers moulded into safety eyewear are not decoration. What the EN 166 family covers, and how each code maps to a specific hazard.
body_html:
Why the marking exists

Safety eyewear sold in Europe carries a compact code, moulded or printed onto the frame and sometimes onto the lens itself. It is not a brand label and not decoration. It is a declaration of which standard the product was tested against and which hazards it is intended to address. Reading it correctly is the difference between wearing eyewear suited to the job and wearing something that merely looks like it.

The parent standard and its family

EN 166 is the general requirements standard for personal eye protection. It covers construction, the field of vision, and the general physical requirements that all eye protectors must meet. It also establishes that a specific filter must satisfy these general requirements in addition to its own.

The hazard-specific members of the family sit beneath it:

  • EN 169 - filters for welding and related techniques, with transmittance requirements and recommended use.
  • EN 170 - ultraviolet filters, with transmittance requirements and recommended use.
  • EN 171 - infrared filters, with transmittance requirements and recommended use.
  • EN 172 - sunglare filters for industrial use, specifying scale numbers and transmittances.

So a product claiming EN 172 is claiming to have been tested as a sunglare filter for industrial use, and it must also satisfy the general requirements of EN 166. A product marked to EN 166 alone is not making a claim about any specific filter type. The distinction matters because a lens can be dark without being a certified sunglare filter, and can be a certified sunglare filter without being impact rated for the task in front of you.

Reading the letters: mechanical strength

The single letters that accompany the standard number describe impact performance. They run from a basic robustness requirement up through low, medium and high energy impact categories, with an additional letter used where the product has also been tested at temperature extremes. A lower-tier letter is not a statement that the eyewear is weak - it means the product was tested and passed against a lesser impact demand. What matters is matching the tier to the hazard. Eyewear rated for low energy impact is not a claim that it will stop everything, and eyewear rated for high energy impact is not automatically the right choice for a chemical splash or a dust problem.

Reading the numbers: optical class and field of use

Two further pieces of information appear in the code. An optical class number describes how much optical distortion the lens introduces: class 1 is the most optically accurate, with higher numbers permitting wider tolerances of power and prism. If you wear the eyewear for long periods rather than for seconds at a time, this is the number worth caring about, because distortion is a fatigue problem before it becomes a safety problem.

A field of use number identifies the specific hazard the protector or filter is intended for - liquid droplets and splashes, coarse dust particles, gas and fine dust, and the other categories defined for the standard. A field of use code is the product telling you what it was designed to stop, which is why the same frame style can exist in several distinctly different specifications, and why two pairs that look identical can carry completely different protective claims.

Why the code is worth reading before you buy

Shop descriptions are written to sell; the marking is written to a test. If you are buying protective eyewear for a workshop, a laboratory, a garden or a bicycle, the marking is the only claim you can check independently. It also travels with the product: a supplier's page may change, but the moulded code on the frame does not.

Where to find the marking, and what it looks like in practice

On spectacles the code usually sits on the temple, with the frame's own product code nearby. On goggles it is generally on the frame body, and where a lens carries a filter marking it may be repeated on the lens itself. A complete marking typically combines a standard number, an optical class number, a mechanical strength letter and one or more field of use numbers, alongside the manufacturer's identification and, for filters, a scale number.

Because these characters are printed small and wear away on working eyewear, it is worth recording the code while the product is new - a photograph of the temple is usually enough - so that you can re-order the same specification later rather than trying to reconstruct it from memory or from a shop listing that may have changed.

Common misconceptions

  • "CE marked means it is safety eyewear." CE marking is a declaration of conformity to the applicable regulation. The EN 166 family code is what tells you the protective claim.
  • "Dark sunglasses protect my eyes at work." Tint is not protection. A dark lens with no filter claim can suppress visible light while letting the hazard through, and sunglasses not intended for industrial use may never have been impact tested at all.
  • "A higher impact rating makes a product better for everything." Impact strength says nothing about chemical splash, molten metal, dust sealing or optical accuracy. Each is a separate claim in the code.
  • "The marking only matters for employers." It is just as useful for DIY, cycling or workshop use, because it is the one claim a shop's marketing text is not required to carry.

When to ask a professional

If you are buying eye protection for a workplace, the required specification should come from the risk assessment for the task, not from the product listing - ask which standards and which codes are mandated for the hazard you actually face. If you need prescription safety eyewear, ask a dispensing optician who supplies certified protective eyewear rather than assuming that an ordinary frame fitted with a certified lens is equivalent, because the frame is part of the protective system. And if you already own protective eyewear whose marking is absent, worn away or unreadable, treat the protective claim as unverified rather than assumed. The marking is the evidence, and no marking means no evidence.

title: Why a Thinner Lens Isn't Always a Lighter One
meta_description: Thickness and weight are different problems. How refractive index, specific gravity and frame size combine to decide how heavy your glasses really feel.
body_html:
Two different problems sold as one

When a higher-index lens is recommended, the reason offered is usually that it will be thinner and lighter. Thinness is a geometric consequence of how steeply a material bends light. Lightness is a different property altogether: it depends on how much the material weighs for a given volume. Those two properties do not move together, and understanding why explains a genuinely counter-intuitive result - a higher-index lens that is visibly thinner than the one you replaced can still weigh more.

Why a higher index makes a lens thinner

A lens has to bend light by the amount your prescription specifies. A material that bends light more strongly per millimetre of curvature needs less curvature to achieve the same power, and less curvature means a flatter, shallower lens. That is the whole basis of the thin-lens ladder: at a given prescription, a lens in a material of refractive index 1.74 is flatter, and therefore thinner at its thickest point, than the same prescription in CR-39 at 1.498.

Verified values for the common materials: CR-39 at 1.498, Trivex at around 1.53, polycarbonate at about 1.586, and the high-index plastics at roughly 1.60, 1.67 and 1.74. Note that the ladder is not evenly spaced - the jump from 1.60 to 1.67 buys less thickness than the jump from 1.498 to 1.60 - which is why the cost of each further step rises faster than the benefit.

Why a higher index often means more weight

The property that governs weight is specific gravity, the density of a material relative to water. It is a separate number from refractive index, and it does not improve as index rises. In practice the pattern is the reverse of what shoppers expect: the impact-resistant materials developed for safety and sport are the lightest of the common options, with polycarbonate and Trivex at the bottom of the density range, ordinary CR-39 in the middle, and higher-index materials generally denser than standard plastic. Mineral glass sits at the top of the range by a wide margin.

So two effects are racing each other. Moving from CR-39 to a much higher index can reduce the lens volume substantially - enough that the weight still falls. But moving one modest step up the index ladder changes the volume only a little while changing the density in the wrong direction, and in that case the lens really can weigh the same or slightly more. Which effect wins depends on your prescription, the size of the lens, and the frame it sits in.

Where the frame enters the calculation

Weight belongs to the finished pair, not to the material. A larger frame needs a larger lens, and lens volume grows with the area of that shape, so a wider frame can add more weight than a lower index would. Decentration matters too, because it determines how much off-centre material the lens has to keep and therefore how thick the edge becomes. This is the quieter half of lens selection, and it is usually the more effective one: choosing a smaller, better-fitting frame often removes more weight than paying for a more expensive material in a large one.

Working out which way the trade-off goes

A simple way to hold both effects at once: moving up the index ladder changes two things, and they pull in opposite directions. The lens becomes flatter, which reduces its volume - a real and often substantial saving at high powers. The material becomes denser, which increases what each unit of that smaller volume weighs. At low and moderate powers the volume is small to begin with, so the density penalty can dominate and the thinner lens ends up no lighter. At high powers there is much more volume to remove, so the flattening effect tends to win. That is the genuine reason index upgrades are recommended for strong prescriptions rather than for everyone, and why an optician who knows your prescription can tell you which side of that trade you are on. If you want to see the thickness half of the calculation for yourself, our free lens thickness calculator compares the common materials at your power.

Common misconceptions

  • "Higher index is always lighter." Not always. Higher-index materials are generally denser, so the saving depends on whether the reduction in volume outweighs the increase in density for your specific prescription.
  • "Thinner lenses are necessarily more comfortable." Comfort depends on weight and on how that weight is balanced on the nose and ears. A thin lens in a large frame can still be heavy and front-heavy.
  • "The index tells you the quality." Index describes how strongly the material bends light. Optical clarity away from the centre is described by the Abbe number, and impact performance by its own set of tests. All three vary independently.
  • "Glass is the premium option." Mineral glass is the densest common material and among the least impact resistant, which is why it has largely been displaced despite excellent optical properties.

When to ask a dispensing optician

Ask about weight rather than thinness if the pair you wear now feels heavy, if you are choosing a large or rimless frame, or if your prescription is strong in one direction only, because the thickest point of a lens and its most visible point are not necessarily in the same place. Ask as well if an index increase has been recommended but your current lenses are not bothering you: in some combinations the change buys a small thickness improvement at a weight cost, and it is entirely fair to ask which of the two you are paying for. And if your spectacles leave marks on your nose or behind your ears, raise that too - frame adjustment and weight distribution usually affect comfort more than any single material decision.

title: Anisometropia: When Your Two Eyes Need Very Different Prescriptions
meta_description: Anisometropia explained: why a difference of 1.00 D or more between your eyes causes more than blur, and how aniseikonia drives the symptoms.
body_html:
What anisometropia actually is

Anisometropia is the term for a difference in refractive error between the two eyes. In clinical use it is usually defined as a difference of 1.00 dioptre or more in spherical equivalent between the right and left eye, although that threshold is a convention rather than a sharp biological boundary. Because both eyes sit in the same head and feed the same visual system, an unequal prescription is not two separate problems. It is one binocular problem.

It helps to picture the scale. In adult eyes, roughly 1 dioptre of refractive difference corresponds to about 0.35–0.40 mm of axial length difference. Half a millimetre of extra eyeball length is a substantial optical difference, and it explains why anisometropia is common in people who are myopic: the longer eye is the more myopic one.

There are three broad patterns, and the distinction matters for what you actually experience:

  • Spherical anisometropia — one eye is more myopic or more hyperopic than the other, equally in all meridians.
  • Astigmatic (cylindrical) anisometropia — the difference is in cylinder power or axis, so the two eyes are blurring in different directions.
  • Antimetropia — a subtype in which one eye is myopic and the other hyperopic. This is the least common and usually the most symptomatic form.

The principle layer: magnification, not just blur

Most people assume the only consequence of an unequal prescription is that one eye sees less clearly. The more important effect is optical and geometric: a spectacle lens changes the size of the image it forms, and it changes it by a different amount for each eye.

This mismatch in perceived image size between the two eyes is called aniseikonia. It is the reason anisometropia causes symptoms that a simple visual acuity test will not detect. Two separate mechanisms drive it:

  • Power magnification — a stronger minus lens minifies more; a stronger plus lens magnifies more. This depends on the lens power itself and on how far it sits from the eye.
  • Shape magnification — a lens with a steeper front curve magnifies. This is why thick, high-curvature lenses feel so different from flat ones.

The useful rule of thumb is that spectacle magnification changes by roughly 1% for every dioptre of power difference, with published estimates ranging from about 0.8% to 1%. That sounds trivial. It is not. Human binocular fusion tolerates only a small percentage of aniseikonia before the brain stops merging the two images comfortably.

Why a lens far from the eye makes it worse

Magnification scales with vertex distance — the gap between the back of the lens and the front of the cornea. Move a strong lens further away and its magnifying or minifying effect grows. This is why contact lenses are often the single most effective fix for anisometropic symptoms: a contact lens sits essentially on the cornea, so vertex distance collapses towards zero and the two retinal images become much closer in size even though the power difference is unchanged.

That is a crucial point and a common source of confusion. The prescription has not changed. The optical consequence of the prescription has changed, because the lens has moved.

What it feels like in practice

Symptoms track the pattern of the mismatch rather than the raw size of the numbers:

  • Headaches and a heavy, strained feeling, typically worse at the end of the day or after sustained reading.
  • A persistent sense that one eye "takes over" while the other feels lazy or suppressed.
  • Difficulty judging distance — pouring liquid into a glass, catching a ball, parking, or walking down stairs.
  • Print that appears to shimmer, or a subtle doubling that disappears when either eye is covered.
  • For large differences, a persistent awareness of the frame edge on one side only.

The stair test is a practical bedside check: if descending stairs feels disproportionately uncertain while both eyes are open but normal with one eye closed, a binocular mismatch is worth investigating.

Common misconceptions

"If both eyes reach 20/20, the prescription is fine." Visual acuity is measured one eye at a time. It says nothing about whether the two images are the same size or whether they fuse comfortably. An anisometropic patient can have perfect acuity in each eye in isolation and still be uncomfortable in binocular use.

"The brain simply adapts." Adaptation is real but partial. The visual system can suppress one image or tolerate a degree of mismatch, and in adults this often means symptoms fade without the underlying asymmetry resolving. In children, though, the same asymmetry can actively interfere with normal visual development — which is why early detection matters far more in paediatric cases than in adults.

"A stronger prescription must mean a better corrected eye." The relevant question is never which eye has the bigger number. It is how different the two numbers are, and how that difference interacts with lens position, lens material and the way the two eyes work together.

"Thinner lenses will fix the discomfort." A higher refractive index reduces thickness, but index also changes the lens curve and affects magnification. Choosing a material purely on cosmetics can move aniseikonia in the wrong direction.

When to see an optometrist or ophthalmologist

Book an assessment if you have a known difference between your eyes and you are experiencing headaches, unreliable depth judgement or a suppressed-feeling eye. Also seek review if a child fails to complain but consistently closes one eye, tilts the head, or performs noticeably worse at distance tasks — children rarely describe anisometropia, and it is one of the causes of amblyopia that screening is designed to catch.

There is also a specific thing to ask about. If your anisometropia was previously well tolerated and has become uncomfortable, the answer may not be a new prescription at all: it may be a change in how far your lenses sit from your eyes, how curved the front of the lens is, or whether a contact lens would suit you better. Those are adjustments an optometrist can make deliberately, and they are worth raising explicitly rather than hoping a routine re-test will land on them by itself.

title: Contrast Sensitivity: Why You Can Pass 20/20 and Still Not See Well
meta_description: Contrast sensitivity explained: why you can pass a 20/20 acuity test and still struggle in low light, and what actually degrades everyday vision.
body_html:
Two different things are being measured

A visual acuity chart measures one very specific ability: resolving high-contrast detail at a small size. Black letters on a white background, sitting at the threshold of being too small to read. When someone says "I have 20/20 vision," that is the only thing that number certifies.

Everyday seeing is almost never like that. Real scenes are full of low-contrast detail — a grey car against grey asphalt in the rain, a step edge in dim stairwells, a face across a dim restaurant, dark text on a dark screen, a curb at dusk. Perceiving those depends on a separate measurement called contrast sensitivity, and the two do not move together.

This is why "but I passed the test" and "but I still can't see properly" can both be true at once. They are answers to different questions.

The principle layer: contrast sensitivity is a curve, not a number

Contrast sensitivity is the ability to detect a pattern as its contrast is reduced. It is usually measured with gratings — alternating light and dark bars — or with letters that become progressively fainter.

The critical concept is spatial frequency, measured in cycles per degree of visual angle. Cycles per degree describes how tightly packed the stripes are within your field of view. Fine detail sits at high spatial frequency; broad, gradual changes sit at low spatial frequency.

Plot sensitivity against spatial frequency and you get the contrast sensitivity function, an inverted U. In normal young adults it peaks in the middle of the range — broadly around 3 to 6 cycles per degree — and falls away at both ends. Published reference intervals put average sensitivity at roughly 2.1 log CS near that peak, dropping towards the high-frequency end of the curve. In plain terms: we are tuned to see medium-sized detail, and we are worse at both the very fine and the very gradual.

Two consequences follow, and both are practical:

  • Acuity tests probe the right-hand tail of the curve. That is why a person can have intact 20/20 acuity and still have depressed contrast sensitivity.
  • Contrast sensitivity is usually measured under low contrast, and the measurement is expressed as log units — on the Pelli-Robson chart, for example. Lower log CS means more contrast is needed before a pattern becomes visible.

What actually degrades it

Contrast sensitivity is a system-level property. It depends on the optics in front of the retina, the retina itself, and the neural processing behind it, so it can be reduced by things that have nothing to do with refractive error:

  • Optical scatter in the eye media. Any haze in the cornea or crystalline lens spreads light sideways and flattens the image before it ever reaches the retina. This is one reason early lens changes can cost contrast sensitivity before they cost acuity.
  • Uncorrected or under-corrected astigmatism. Cylinder error smears the image in one meridian, which hits medium spatial frequencies hardest — the very region the eye is normally best at.
  • Light scatter at the lens surface. Surface reflections and a dirty, smeared or badly scratched lens add veiling glare. This is a large part of what an anti-reflective coating buys you.
  • Pupil size and light level. In dim light the pupil widens, which admits more aberrations, and the retina itself becomes less sensitive. Night vision is a genuinely lower-contrast regime.
  • Ageing. The neural and optical contributions both decline with age, and reduced contrast sensitivity is one of the more reliable age-related changes in visual function.
  • Dry eye and tear film instability. An irregular tear film is an irregular optical surface, and it degrades the image intermittently — which is why vision that fluctuates with blinking is a classic sign.

Common misconceptions

"20/20 means my vision is perfect." It means your high-contrast resolution is normal at that distance. It is a threshold measurement, not a description of visual quality.

"If contrast is poor, I need a stronger prescription." Often the prescription is already correct. Improving contrast perception usually means addressing the other contributors: correcting residual astigmatism, managing tear film, reducing surface reflections, or working in adequate light.

"A darker tint must make things clearer." Tint reduces the total light reaching the retina. In bright conditions that can improve comfort, but a dark lens in dim conditions lowers contrast — it works against you. Lens tint is a light-level solution, not a contrast solution.

"Scratches are only cosmetic." Deep scratches scatter light and produce localised loss of contrast in the affected area of the field. A lens can be optically correct and still perform poorly because of surface condition.

When to see an optometrist or ophthalmologist

Raise it if your acuity is reported as normal but you still struggle in low light, in rain or fog, on stairs, or when reading low-contrast text — and say so explicitly, because contrast sensitivity is not part of a routine refraction and is usually only tested when someone asks or when a specific condition is suspected.

Seek prompt assessment if reduced contrast sensitivity appears suddenly or asymmetrically between the two eyes, if it comes with glare or halos around lights, or if colours look washed out or different between eyes. Those patterns point towards causes that need examination rather than a lens change, and they should not be managed by ordering a new pair of glasses and hoping.

Practically, if you are choosing lenses and care about seeing well in poor conditions rather than only in good ones, ask what the lens does about scatter. Surface quality, coating choice and accurate correction of astigmatism usually matter more to real-world contrast than a change in index or a tint.

title: Bifocal Segment Designs Explained: Flat-Top, Round and Executive
meta_description: Bifocal segment designs compared: flat-top, round and executive lenses, and how segment optical centre and image jump change what you actually feel.
body_html:
The part of a bifocal that nobody explains

A bifocal lens has two optical powers cut into one piece of material. Almost all the discussion around them focuses on that fact — distance on top, reading below. What gets skipped is the thing that actually determines how a bifocal feels to wear: the geometry of the reading segment, and in particular where its optical centre sits relative to the line you are looking through.

Two patients can be given "bifocals with a +2.00 add" printed on the same order and have completely different experiences, because the segment design was different.

The principle layer: optical centre and image jump

Every lens has an optical centre — the point through which light passes undeviated. Looking away from that point introduces prism, and the amount of prism grows with the distance from the centre.

When you drop your gaze from the distance portion into the reading segment, your line of sight crosses the segment boundary and immediately transfers to the segment's own optical centre. If that centre is not sitting where your line of sight lands, the eye receives an abrupt step of prism at the boundary. That abrupt step is called image jump.

Your eye does not smoothly transition. It jumps, and the two images — one through the distance portion, one through the segment — are displaced relative to each other. The size of the jump depends almost entirely on how far the segment's optical centre is from the top edge of the segment, because that is the edge your gaze crosses.

This is where the designs separate cleanly:

  • Flat-top (D-segment or straight-top). The most widely used design. The segment has a straight horizontal top edge with a rounded bottom, giving a shape like a capital D. Common widths are 22 mm, 25 mm and 28 mm. Critically, the optical centre of the segment sits about 5 mm below the top line. That offset is what creates image jump — but it is also what makes the design practical, because the segment is wide and shallow, so a normal reading posture uses it comfortably.
  • Round segment. A circular reading segment. The optical centre sits at the geometric centre of that circle. Because the segment is small and its centre is deep inside it, the jump behaviour differs from a flat-top — and the useable reading area is narrower, which is why round segments are less common in general dispensing.
  • Executive (Franklin). The original bifocal construction, and still the one that behaves most like two lenses joined. The dividing line runs the full width of the lens, and the reading portion occupies the entire lower half. There is effectively no image jump at the boundary, because there is no discontinuous shift of optical centre. The trade-offs are appearance, cost and thickness, not optics.

The pattern is worth stating plainly: a smaller, tucked-away segment generally means more image jump and less reading area; a full-width segment means less jump but a much more visible lens. Design is a compromise, not a hierarchy.

What the numbers mean on an order form

A bifocal order typically specifies the segment width — "28 flat top", for example — and separately a segment height, which is the vertical position of the segment's top edge measured from the bottom of the lens frame, or referenced to the pupil. Segment height is the single most consequential number in the whole order, and it is a fitting decision rather than a prescription decision. Put it too low and the patient has to tilt their head down and look under the segment to read. Put it too high and the segment intrudes on distance vision, appearing as a visible line across the middle of the field.

This is also why bifocals cannot sensibly be bought by measuring your own eyes at home. The prescription can be copied. The segment height cannot, because it depends on where your pupils sit in that specific frame on your specific face.

Common misconceptions

"Bifocals are obsolete; everyone should get progressives." Progressives remove the visible line and the image jump, but they introduce peripheral aberration and a narrower corridor of clear vision. For some tasks and some wearers — particularly people who want a wide, stable reading area and do not mind the line — a flat-top bifocal genuinely performs better. It is a different compromise, not an older one.

"The line is what causes the jump." The visible line is an appearance feature. The jump comes from the position of the segment's optical centre relative to the boundary. An executive bifocal has a very obvious line and essentially no jump.

"A bigger segment is always better." A wider segment trades away distance vision and increases lens thickness and weight at the bottom edge. The right width depends on the reading task and the frame depth.

"If it feels wrong, the add power is wrong." A wrong-feeling bifocal is at least as likely to be a segment height or centration problem as a power problem — and those are fixed by re-measuring the fit, not by changing the prescription.

When to see an optometrist or ophthalmologist

Go back to your optometrist if you find yourself lifting your chin, tilting your head, or repeatedly looking above or below the segment to read. Those are fit problems, and they are usually measurable and correctable.

If a bifocal produces double vision, a persistent pulling sensation, or a feeling that your eyes are fighting each other, have it assessed rather than adapting around it. Those symptoms can indicate that the prism imbalance between the two portions of the lens is not being tolerated, and in some cases they point to a binocular vision issue that deserves proper examination rather than a lens tweak.

And if you are choosing between a bifocal and a progressive, the honest framing is that you are choosing which set of compromises you would rather live with. Ask to see the segment options and how they sit on your face — the geometry, not the marketing, is what you will actually feel.

title: Decentration and Minimum Blank Size: How a Lens Is Fitted to Your Frame
meta_description: Decentration and minimum blank size explained: how optical centres are moved to your pupils, and why frame choice changes how thick your lenses look.
body_html:
The invisible step between your prescription and your lenses

You hand over a prescription with two numbers for each eye. Some days later you collect a pair of glasses. In between, a set of geometric decisions was made that never appear on the prescription and are rarely discussed at the counter — decisions that determine whether the optical centre of each lens actually lands in front of your pupil, how thick the edges end up, and whether the lens could even be cut to fit the frame you chose.

The two concepts at the centre of that process are decentration and minimum blank size. Understanding them explains a lot of otherwise mysterious outcomes, including why one frame costs far more than another with an identical prescription.

The principle layer: the optical centre must move to the pupil

A finished lens is manufactured as a round blank whose optical centre sits at its geometric centre. In a perfectly symmetric world, you would cut the lens so that this optical centre ends up exactly in front of the pupil, and everything would be simple.

Real frames are not symmetric. The distance between the two lens apertures — the frame pupillary distance — is a property of the frame, and it rarely equals your own pupillary distance. So the optical centre has to be shifted sideways, inwards or outwards, to line up with your eye. That shift is decentration, and it is a deliberate, calculated operation, not an accident of cutting.

The arithmetic is straightforward once you have the numbers:

  • Frame PD = A + DBL, where A is the horizontal width of one lens aperture and DBL is the bridge width (the distance between lenses). Both are usually stamped on the inside of the temple.
  • Decentration per lens = (Frame PD − your PD) ÷ 2.

Work an example. A frame marked 52–18 has a frame PD of 70 mm. If your own pupillary distance is 64 mm, the difference is 6 mm, so each lens must be decentred by 3 mm — inwards, because the frame is wider than your face.

Why blank size decides what is possible

Decentring a lens means moving the optical centre away from the blank's centre. That movement consumes material, and how much material is available is set by the blank's diameter. The controlling dimension is the ED — the effective diameter, meaning the longest straight line across the lens aperture as it will be cut, which for many shapes is a diagonal rather than the horizontal width.

A standard working rule for the smallest blank that will do the job is:

  • Minimum blank size = ED + (2 × decentration) + 2 mm

The trailing 2 mm is allowance for the edging process itself. Continue the example: if the ED for that frame is 54 mm and decentration is 3 mm per lens, the minimum blank is 54 + 6 + 2 = 62 mm. A 65 mm blank will do it comfortably. A 60 mm blank simply will not, no matter what the prescription says, and the lens would have to be made specially.

This is the mechanical reason that a very wide frame on a narrow face, or a very wide frame combined with a high prescription, can become unexpectedly expensive. The geometry demands a bigger blank, and bigger high-index blanks cost more.

How this connects to thickness

Decentration and thickness are directly linked, because moving the optical centre towards the edge of the blank means the cut lens includes more of the region where the surface curves away. For a minus lens, that is more edge thickness; for a plus lens, more centre thickness. Two people with identical prescriptions can therefore collect noticeably different-looking glasses purely because of frame choice and PD — and the person with the wider frame is usually the one with the thicker edge.

If you want to see how prescription, index and frame size interact before you order, the site's lens thickness calculator gives an estimate from those inputs. Treat the result as an estimate for comparison shopping rather than a dispensing value, which is exactly what it is designed to be.

Common misconceptions

"Smaller frames mean thinner lenses, so always choose small." Smaller apertures do generally reduce edge thickness for minus prescriptions, but they can also reduce the field of view and make the frame uncomfortable. There is a balance point, and it depends on your PD as well as your power.

"The lab can always cut any lens into any frame." If the minimum blank size exceeds what is available in that material and index, it genuinely cannot be done as a standard job. This is a hard geometric limit, not a matter of effort.

"Decentration is a way of hiding a wrong PD." Decentration is calculated from a correct PD. If the PD used is wrong, decentring compounds the error — it does not correct it. This is one reason an inaccurate self-measured PD can produce glasses that feel slightly wrong even when the prescription itself is right.

"Optical centre just means the middle of the lens." It means the point of zero prism. Where it needs to be placed is determined by your pupils; where it sits by default is the middle of the blank. Those are different locations, and closing the gap between them is the whole point of the process.

When to see an optometrist or ophthalmologist

Ask for your PD and your frame measurements to be recorded properly if you are ordering glasses online, and be sceptical of a single PD copied from an old order if your frame has changed substantially.

Return for a re-check if new glasses cause a pulling or drifting sensation, if one eye feels strained while the other does not, or if you find yourself turning your head to look through the centre of the lens. Those can be centration symptoms rather than power symptoms, and they are diagnosed by measuring where the optical centres actually sit in the finished pair — something an optometrist can check directly on the assembled glasses.

If you have a high prescription, a large difference between your eyes, or a strong cylinder, mention the frame you are considering before ordering. The right time to discover that a frame demands a larger blank than usual is while there is still a choice to make.

title: Free-Form Lenses: How Digital Surfacing Makes a Lens to Your Exact Prescription
meta_description: Free-form lens surfacing explained: how point-by-point CNC cutting puts the prescription on the back surface, and what changes for high powers.
body_html:
The lens you receive is not the lens that was ordered

A spectacle lens starts life as a semi-finished blank: a disc of material with one optical surface already formed by the manufacturer and the other left flat, waiting. The prescription is not the blank. The prescription is what the laboratory cuts into that flat second side, in a process called surfacing. Understanding surfacing explains a whole category of things patients notice but rarely get explained — why two pairs with identical numbers can perform differently, why a lens sometimes has a visibly different curve than expected, and why a "free-form" or "digital" lens carries a premium.

Why the back surface became the important one

Traditional lens manufacturing used moulds and fixed curve sets. The front surface carried the base curve, and the laboratory picked the closest available semi-finished blank and cut the back to hit the prescription. Because the front surface was a fixed catalogue curve, the design had to be chosen from what existed, and the lab worked within the tolerance of a stepped curve system.

Digital, or free-form, surfacing changed that relationship. Instead of a cutting tool following a fixed spherical arc, a computer-controlled generator cuts the surface point by point, producing a shape that departs from rotational symmetry. That means the front surface can stay whatever it needs to be, and the entire optical design — sphere, cylinder, axis, prism and any progressive corridor — can be placed on the back surface. The two surfaces are then no longer competing for control of the optics.

What actually changes for the wearer

The practical differences show up in a few predictable places:

  • High and asymmetric prescriptions. When sphere and cylinder are both large, or when the two eyes differ considerably, the ability to place the full prescription independently on one surface matters far more than any single design advantage.
  • Asphericity and flattening. A free-form back surface can carry the correction while the front stays relatively flat, which is what makes flatter, thinner-looking lenses possible without introducing the edge distortion an equivalent front-side design would bring.
  • Position of wear. Because the surface is calculated rather than chosen from a catalogue, the calculation can include the geometry in which the glasses will actually sit on the face — the distance from lens to eye, the tilt of the frame on the nose, and the height at which the frame sits in front of the pupil.
  • Progressive designs. A progressive corridor is inherently an asymmetric free-form shape. Cutting it directly is fundamentally different from blending it into a fixed front curve.

The tolerances that still apply

Free-form does not mean unbounded precision. Finished lenses still have to meet the applicable finished-lens standards, and for progressive lenses in particular the relevant family is ISO 8980, which sets the tolerances for the power measured at specified points on the lens. A lens can be cut to a fraction of a dioptre of the intended design and still be judged on how it performs at the reference points the standard defines. In other words: the manufacturing method and the acceptance criteria are two different things, and a better method does not exempt a lens from the standard.

Common misconceptions

"Free-form always means better vision." It means the surface can be made more precisely to a specified design. If the prescribed design does not suit how you use your eyes, making it more exactly will not help — it will make the mismatch more exact. The largest gains are concentrated in high power, high cylinder, and asymmetric prescriptions, and in progressive designs.

"Digital lenses are just marketing for the same product." The two processes are genuinely different: one selects from curved blanks and grinds within that constraint, the other computes and cuts a surface point by point. Whether the difference is visible to a particular wearer is a separate question — and the honest answer is that for a simple, low-power single-vision lens the difference can be small.

"A more precise lens means no adaptation period." Precision in manufacture does not remove the adaptation that comes from a changed optical design. A precisely made progressive is still a progressive, and the corridors and peripheral zones that make it what it is do not disappear because the surface is more exact.

"If the lens is custom-made, the lab measurements cannot be wrong." The calculation is only as good as the position-of-wear data fed into it. If the measurements taken at the fitting are wrong, a free-form lens will faithfully implement the wrong geometry.

Lens thickness and material

Surfacing and material choice interact directly. A higher refractive index material allows the same power with a flatter curve, and that flatter curve carries less sagitta — the depth of the curve — which is what determines how far the edge of a minus lens or the centre of a plus lens projects. This is the mechanism behind "thinner" lenses, and it is worth separating from "lighter": the two follow different physical causes. If you want to see how index and lens size interact with edge thickness, the site's lens thickness calculator lets you vary those inputs directly.

When to raise it with your optician or optometrist

Ask about the surfacing method when your prescription is high or highly asymmetric, when you have struggled with progressives before, or when two apparently identical pairs have behaved differently. Also ask how the position-of-wear measurements were taken — if they were not taken at all, the custom surface has less to work with. Persistent distortion, unequal image sizes between the eyes, or a difference that does not settle within a couple of weeks are reasons to go back for a recheck rather than to accept it, and any sudden change in vision should be assessed professionally rather than adjusted around.

title: Presbyopia: Why Your Near Point Moves Away After 40
