meta_description: Presbyopia explained: how the crystalline lens stiffens, why accommodation declines about 0.23 D a year, and what the near point really measures.
body_html:
The autofocus you never noticed having

Look up from this page at something across the room. Your eyes refocused, and you felt nothing happen. That adjustment is accommodation, and it is the reason presbyopia exists as a separate problem from long-sightedness. A camera changes focus by moving a lens group. The human eye changes focus by changing the shape of a single lens, and that lens becomes less willing to change shape as the years pass.

The mechanism: a lens that stiffens as it grows

The crystalline lens sits behind the iris, suspended by a ring of fibres called the zonules, which connect it to the ciliary body. In the classic description, contraction of the ciliary muscle slackens the zonules and lets the lens spring into a rounder, more powerful shape for near vision; relaxation pulls the zonules taut and flattens the lens for distance.

The key structural fact is that the lens keeps growing throughout life. New fibres are laid down in shells, like the rings of a tree, and the older, denser material is compressed toward the centre. The result is a lens that becomes thicker and stiffer with age. A stiffer lens cannot change shape as far for the same muscular effort, and the capsule that encloses it also changes its properties. Accommodation therefore declines not because the focusing muscle weakens, but because the lens itself becomes progressively less deformable — a mechanical limit rather than a muscular one.

The numbers: amplitude and the near point

The clinical quantity is the amplitude of accommodation: the difference in optical power the eye can add, measured in dioptres, between its fully relaxed state and its maximum effort. It is closely tied to the near point — the closest distance at which something can be held and still be seen sharply. The dioptric equivalent of a near point distance in centimetres is 100 divided by that distance, so a near point of 25 cm corresponds to 4 dioptres of accommodation in use.

Amplitude declines steadily and predictably. Published figures vary with measurement method — subjective push-up testing and objective techniques do not agree perfectly — but the shape of the curve is consistent. One large adult study reported an average amplitude of roughly 7.5 dioptres in the 35–40 age band with a decline of about 0.23 dioptres per year. Historical clinical reports, including Duane's early work, placed the usual age of onset in the range of about 38 to 48 years, and modern reviews note that the amplitude is close to fully lost by the early-to-mid fifties.

Why the forties are the tipping point

Near vision does not need the full amplitude. Comfortable sustained reading typically uses something in the region of the closer half of the available range, because holding focus at the absolute limit is fatiguing. That reserve is what makes the arithmetic work out the way it does: at a comfortable 40 cm reading distance the eye needs about 2.5 dioptres in use. Somewhere in the early forties the remaining amplitude, minus a workable reserve, stops covering that demand for any length of time. The person has not lost a skill they once had; they have run out of margin.

This also explains two details that surprise people. First, that presbyopia starts with fatigue and with holding things further away, not with an abrupt blur. Second, that it progresses: the same person who needed a small reading addition at 44 typically needs a larger one at 55, because the underlying amplitude keeps falling.

It is also worth separating presbyopia from hyperopia. Someone who is long-sighted has been compensating with accommodation all along, so their reserve runs out earlier and presbyopia can become noticeable in the late thirties. Someone who is short-sighted may find they can still read comfortably without any correction by removing their distance glasses — not because their lens has stayed flexible, but because the myopic defocus happens to land the near point at a usable distance.

Common misconceptions

"Presbyopia is a disease of the eye muscles." The focusing muscle is generally still capable. The limiting factor is the stiffening of the lens itself, which is why exercises do not restore a lost amplitude and why the change keeps progressing regardless of effort.

"Reading glasses will make my eyes weaker." Using a reading addition does not accelerate the underlying loss of amplitude, which is structural. It is common to need a stronger addition later, and that reflects the underlying progression, not the use of the glasses.

"Everyone becomes presbyopic at exactly 40." Onset is a range, not a date. It depends on the refractive error, on working distance, on how much sustained near work the person does, and on individual anatomy. Two people the same age can differ by years.

"Over-the-counter readers are the same thing as a proper prescription." Ready-made readers give the same power to both eyes and take no account of astigmatism, of a difference between the two eyes, or of the distance at which you actually work. They can work well for a straightforward case and poorly for an asymmetric one.

When to see an optometrist or ophthalmologist

See a professional for a proper refraction when near vision starts to limit what you do, when you find yourself extending your arms to read, or when headaches and eye strain appear after close work. Do not self-select a strength by guessing from a shop display — the addition depends on your distance prescription and your working distance, and it needs measuring.

Some changes are not ordinary presbyopia and should be assessed rather than worked around: a sudden change in near vision, vision that differs markedly between the two eyes, distortion rather than simple blur, or any loss of vision that develops quickly. A routine eye examination also checks the health of the eye itself, which is a separate matter from how well it focuses.

title: Hydrophobic and Oleophobic Coatings: The Outermost Layer on Your Lens
meta_description: What the hydrophobic and oleophobic topcoat does: surface energy and water contact angle, and why this thinnest layer is the first one to wear out.
body_html:
The last layer applied and the first one touched

A modern lens surface is a stack. Underneath are the hard coat and the anti-reflective layers; on top sits the thinnest layer of all, the hydrophobic and oleophobic topcoat. It is also the layer that takes every fingerprint, every wipe and every cleaning spray. Understanding what this layer does physically — and what it cannot do — explains a great deal about why lenses seem to become harder to keep clean as they age.

The principle: surface energy decides what water does

Whether water beads up or spreads out on a surface is governed by the surface energy of that surface and the resulting contact angle — the angle at which a droplet meets the surface. A high-energy surface pulls the water flat and lets it spread into a film. A low-energy surface repels the droplet, holding it in a tight bead with a high contact angle.

The convention is straightforward: a surface is described as hydrophobic when the water contact angle exceeds about 90 degrees, and superhydrophobic when it exceeds roughly 150 degrees. On a lens, the practical goal is not to make water vanish but to make it form tight beads that roll or flick away instead of smearing into a film that has to be wiped — because it is the wiping, not the water, that puts fine scratches into a lens over years of use.

Two different jobs that are often spoken of as one

The two words in the name describe two different targets:

  • Hydrophobic means it repels water. This is what makes rain bead and run off, and what keeps a lens from holding a film of condensation.
  • Oleophobic means it repels oils. Skin oil from fingers and from the brow is the actual problem in daily wear, because oil spreads into a thin film that is far harder to remove than water and is what produces the smeared look after an apparently good clean.

A coating that handles water well but not oil will still smear. In practice the topcoat chemistry is chosen to lower surface energy against both, which is why the two terms travel together even though they are separate properties.

Note what this layer is not. The anti-reflective part of the stack works by optical interference — thin layers arranged so that reflections cancel. The topcoat is not there for that purpose; it modifies the surface, not the interference. Similarly, a hydrophobic topcoat is not the same thing as an anti-fog coating. Anti-fog surfaces go the opposite way: they are hydrophilic, deliberately high-energy, so that condensation spreads into an invisible film rather than beading into scattering droplets. A surface cannot be strongly hydrophobic and anti-fog at the same time. This is why combination products have to compromise, and why a lens marketed for both rarely excels at either.

Why the topcoat wears out first

Several things work against this layer, and they compound:

  • Mechanical abrasion. Every wipe moves a cloth across the outermost surface. Even a clean microfibre cloth imposes some wear, and a dry wipe over grit imposes a great deal more.
  • Cleaning chemistry. Solvents, alcohol-based sprays, detergents and particularly abrasive household cleaners attack or strip a low-energy layer more readily than they attack the hard coat beneath it.
  • Soaps and lotions. Residues from hand soap and skin products deposit oils and surfactants onto the very surface that is supposed to repel them, occupying the sites that would otherwise shed water.
  • Heat. Leaving glasses on a car dashboard or in a hot environment is unkind to thin films in general.

The observable symptom is gradual: a lens that beaded water when new starts holding a streak, and cleaning requires more rubbing to achieve less. That is a surface property degrading, not a sign that the lens no longer corrects vision.

Common misconceptions

"The coating stops my glasses fogging up." A hydrophobic topcoat repels water droplets; it does not prevent condensation, and it can actually encourage beading when the lens is cold. Fogging is a temperature and humidity problem, and the surfaces designed to address it use the opposite surface chemistry.

"A hydrophobic coating means I don't need to clean carefully." The coating reduces how often you need to wipe, but the wiping is what removes the coating. Bothering less is not the same as being able to clean harshly.

"Anti-reflective and hydrophobic are the same upgrade." They are different layers doing different jobs, and the outer one is often applied on top of the inner one during manufacture. Losing the topcoat does not remove the anti-reflective performance; it removes the easy-clean behaviour.

"I can restore the coating with a spray." There are aftermarket treatments that temporarily re-establish water repellency, and they can genuinely help, but they are a top-up on the surface rather than a rebuild of the bonded layer, and they typically need reapplying. Any product that claims to restore a coating by polishing the lens is far more likely to be removing material than adding it.

When to raise it with your optician or optometrist

Ask about the coating specification when ordering, particularly if you know from experience that you are hard on lenses, and ask what cleaning method is recommended for that particular stack — the advice for a coated lens is not the same as for an uncoated one. If a lens has become persistently smeary within a short time of purchase, that is a reasonable thing to raise with the supplier rather than to live with.

Separately, coating wear is not the same as a vision problem. If vision itself has changed, or if a lens is scratched deeply enough to scatter light, the question is no longer cosmetic and belongs with an eye care professional rather than a cleaning routine.
